Punk
PUNK
noun / adjective (Gen X slang)
An old English word of uncertain origin with a disreputable history: in Shakespeare’s day a punk was a harlot; by the early 20th century American slang used it for a worthless young man, a petty hoodlum, or a coward ("to punk out," to back down), the sense Clint Eastwood made famous in Dirty Harry (1971). American rock critics of the early 1970s applied punk rock to raw 1960s garage bands; then Punk magazine (New York, 1976), the Ramones’ first album (1976), the club CBGB, and in London the Sex Pistols’ "Anarchy in the U.K." (1976) and "God Save the Queen" (1977) fixed it as the name of a loud, fast, defiant music and its look: safety pins, torn shirts, spiked or Mohawk hair, and a do-it-yourself ethic.

Biblical Definition

Punk had two meanings for Gen X. The older one was an insult: a punk was a young hood, a loudmouth, or a coward who talks tough and then runs. The newer one was a badge: a punk was a kid who played three-chord songs as fast as possible, cut his own hair, made his own records, and sneered at the system. The movement’s slogans were anarchy and "no future," and some of its early records mocked the crown and the church on purpose. The Christian observation is that the Bible has seen anarchy before and does not admire it: "In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes" (Jdg 21:25). Proverbs describes a whole "generation that curseth their father, and doth not bless their mother" (Pro 30:11), and Samuel warned a king that "rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft" (1Sa 15:23). But punk also smelled something true: that the respectable world was often hollow, that conformity is not the same as righteousness. Scripture’s nonconformity goes deeper than any safety pin: "be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind" (Rom 12:2). And God has a habit of choosing the misfits: "God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise" (1Co 1:27). A father can tell his son: you want to be a rebel? Rebel against the flesh, the world, and the devil. That is the only revolution that lasts, and its King was crucified for leading it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Old slang for a hoodlum or coward, reborn in 1976–77 (Ramones, Sex Pistols) as the name of fast, defiant rock and its do-it-yourself tribe; Scripture rejects anarchy (Jdg 21:25) and offers a deeper nonconformity (Rom 12:2).

PUNK, n. and adj. (Gen X slang, 1976–77, New York and London) A fast, loud, stripped-down style of rock music; a follower of it, known by torn clothes, safety pins, and spiked or Mohawk hair; anything defiantly anti-establishment. "He’s been punk since seventh grade."

Punk rock, punk rocker, hardcore punk (early 1980s), pop punk, post-punk; the DIY ethic of self-made records and zines.

Older senses still alive: a petty hoodlum or worthless young man; a coward ("to punk out"); Elizabethan, a harlot.

Webster 1828: PUNK, n. A prostitute; a strumpet.

Decode for parents: punk often begins as a hunger for honesty; turn the rebellion against sin rather than against parents.

Key Scripture

Jdg 21:25 — "In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes."

Pro 30:11 — "There is a generation that curseth their father, and doth not bless their mother."

1Sa 15:23 — "For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry. Because thou hast rejected the word of the LORD, he hath also rejected thee from being king."

Rom 12:2 — "And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God."

1Co 1:27 — "But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;"

Modern Corruption

Punk made rebellion a style and anarchy a slogan; Scripture names rebellion as the sin of witchcraft and offers the only true nonconformity — a mind transformed by God.

expand to see more

Anarchy as identity. The punk slogan was that no one should rule, and the Bible has a book that shows what that looks like: Judges, where every man did what was right in his own eyes (Jdg 21:25) and the land fell apart. Rebellion against all authority is not freedom but the oldest sin in a new haircut; Samuel ranked it with witchcraft (1Sa 15:23). A movement that taught a generation to curse father and mother (Pro 30:11) left many of its children with exactly the "no future" it chanted.

What punk got right. Yet punk’s contempt for fakery, its do-it-yourself grit, and its refusal to be a consumer are not far from the kingdom. The Christian is the real nonconformist, transformed rather than conformed (Rom 12:2), and God loves to build His church out of people the respectable world wrote off — the foolish, the weak, the base (1Co 1:27). The cure for a punk is not a necktie but a cause big enough to give his life to.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Elizabethan punk (harlot) → American hoodlum / coward (early 1900s) → Dirty Harry (1971) → punk rock (1970s critics) → Ramones and Sex Pistols (1976–77); Scripture: be not conformed (Rom 12:2).

Late 16th c. punk — a harlot; origin uncertain

Early 20th c. US: a worthless young man, hoodlum, or coward; punk out

Early 1970s rock criticism: punk rock for raw garage bands

1976–77: Punk magazine, the Ramones, CBGB, the Sex Pistols; safety pins and Mohawks

Biblical nonconformity: be ye transformed (Rom 12:2); God chooses the foolish things (1Co 1:27)

Usage

"Every man did that which was right in his own eyes (Jdg 21:25) — anarchy is not new."

"Be not conformed to this world (Rom 12:2) — the rebellion worth joining."
